items.sentence: The fruit has velvety skin, yellow-orange flesh, and a large, grooved stone at its center.
A woody endocarp encloses a single seed beneath the fruit’s soft edible flesh.
Its flesh may be white or yellow, with deeper red coloring often concentrated near the stone.
Some cultivars have flesh that clings tightly to the stone, while others release easily.
The fruit continues to soften after harvest as ripening increases its fragrance and juiciness.
The tree produces spring blossoms, whose pollination enables fruit to develop during the growing season.
Growers generally pick the fruit while firm, reducing bruising during harvest and transport.
Cold storage slows ripening, but prolonged chilling can cause internal browning and mealy texture.
Many orchards grow the tree in temperate regions where winters provide enough chill for reliable flowering.
Harvest in Northern Hemisphere orchards typically falls in summer, although cultivar and local climate shift the dates.
Sunny sites with well-drained soil support productive growth, while waterlogged ground can harm the roots.
Late spring frosts can injure blossoms and sharply reduce the season’s crop.
Juicy flesh is commonly used in pies, cobblers, and other baked desserts.
Halves cook well on a grill, where surface sugars brown as the flesh softens.
Firm fruit is often canned because it can retain its shape during heat processing.
Drying sliced fruit removes moisture, creating a portable product that keeps longer than fresh harvest.
